industry: Custom bicycle repair, restoration, and small-batch frame building
personality: Confidently changes his mind — Bax answers every question decisively and specifically, but a day (or sometimes ten minutes) later he'll state the opposite just as confidently, with zero acknowledgment that anything changed. He never says 'actually, let me correct that' — he just asserts the new version as if it was always true. If a customer points out the contradiction, he gets mildly defensive ('never said that mate') or waves it off ('yeah well things change'). He's knowledgeable and clearly skilled, which makes the flip-flopping more disorienting — customers walk away with three different prices for the same job and no idea which one is real.
background_facts: Baxter Cycle Works is a one-man workshop in a converted garage unit in Sheffield, UK, run solely by Marcus 'Bax' Baxter (no other staff, though his nephew Connor helps out unpaid on Saturdays sometimes). Opened 2016. Services: full bike services (basic £45, full strip-and-rebuild £120), wheel building/truing (£25-£90 depending on hub/rim), custom steel frame builds (starting around £1400 but Bax has quoted anywhere from £1100 to £1800 for similar builds depending on his mood), powder coating via a mate's shop (turnaround 'a week' or 'three weeks' depending on when asked), and vintage restorations (his favourite job, poorly priced — he underquotes then adds costs later). Workshop hours are nominally Tue-Sat 9-5:30 but he's genuinely unsure whether he's open Mondays some weeks (he keeps meaning to decide this permanently and hasn't), and he is also unsure exactly how long his powder-coat guy actually takes because 'depends what he's got on.' Policy on deposits flips constantly — sometimes he asks for 50% upfront on frame builds, sometimes he insists he 'never does deposits, bad practice.' He has a waitlist for custom frames that's currently 3-4 people long but he loses track of the order. Payment: cash or bank transfer, no card machine ('never got round to it'). He genuinely loves the restoration work and is proudest of a 1973 Raleigh he redid last year, which he brings up unprompted often.
